newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus politicians debate Rifkind visit.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus politicians debate Rifkind visit.

text.p: Cypriot politicians, angered by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind's plan to go to Turkish-held northern Cyprus during a visit to the island next week, will discuss the matter with the Cypriot president on Wednesday, an official said on Monday.
"There is no issue of Mr. Rifkind postponing his visit," government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides told reporters.

Three political parties have expressed concern at Rifkind's intention of visiting Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash in the north, fearing this could imply British recognition of the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state there.

Cassoulides said President Glafcos Clerides's government, which gave its consent to Rifkind's visit with Denktash in northern Cyprus, had agreed to hear objections by party leaders at an all-party meeting on Wednesday.
Rifkind, who will become the first British foreign secretary to visit the former British colony since its independence in 1960, has a scheduled meeting with Clerides.
Discussions will focus on the prospects for a achieving a comprehensive negotiated settlement of the Cyprus problem in 1997, before it starts negotiations to join the European Union.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 and occupied its northern third after a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the military ruling Greece. A breakaway state the Greek Cypriots declared there in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara.
Local opposition to Rifkind's visit to northern Cyprus has been spearheaded by Spyros Kyprianou, leader of the centre-right Democratic Party and chairman of the House of Representatives.
"This constitutes indirect recognition and it is totally unacceptable for this visit to take place in my opinion," said Kyprianou, whose party is a junior partner in the government.
Rifkind touched a raw nerve two weeks ago when he claimed in the House of Commons that Cyprus's accession to the EU would be "extremely difficult" before a settlement to the Cyprus.
Cyprus is due to embark on accession negotiations with the EU in around 12 months' time, irrespective of whether the political problem is solved or not.
"The national council will examine the views put forward by party leaders....We would be happier if this visit had taken place without the comments which preceeded it," Cassoulides said.
